exp: A K-map for 4 variables has 2^4 = 16 cells (one per minterm combination).
A multiplexer takes several input lines plus a set of selection lines and routes exactly one of the inputs to a single output line, matching the description exactly.
Block/buffer caches hold recently used disk blocks in memory so repeat reads avoid the slower disk access, improving overall disk I/O performance.

A linking loader resolves external references and combines separately compiled object modules into one executable image; an assembler only turns source into object code, and a cross compiler targets a different machine.
An XOR gate outputs 1 when the number of 1-inputs is odd, so cascading XOR gates over a word's bits directly tests odd parity.

An encoder is the circuit that produces a specific binary code/word as its output when one of its many input lines is active; a decoder does the reverse (binary word in, one line out), so it doesn't fit 'produces a binary word'.
A demultiplexer takes a single input and, using select lines, routes it to one of many outputs; option (b) describes a multiplexer instead.
In a PAL (Programmable Array Logic), the AND array is programmable (fuses define product terms) while the OR array is fixed, which is the opposite of a PLA.
Asynchronous inputs such as preset/clear act immediately and override the synchronous (clock-driven) behaviour of a flip-flop.
In asynchronous (start-stop) transmission the line idles at logic high (mark); the start bit is the transition to logic low that signals the beginning of a character.
Cascaded counters divide the clock by the product of their moduli: 48 kHz / (6*4) = 48 kHz / 24 = 2 kHz.

A ripple-carry (parallel) adder adds multiple bit positions of two numbers together in one pass (carries ripple through), unlike a half-/full-adder which handles a single bit position, or a serial adder which processes one bit per clock cycle.
The maximum frequency at which data can reliably be clocked into a gate, limited by its propagation delay, is referred to as its operating speed; the other terms aren't standard names for this limit.

For the basic gated (D) latch, collapsing the input combinations that give the same next-state behaviour yields a primitive flow table with 3 stable total-states/rows; this is a narrow textbook-specific fact and I'm not fully certain the source text uses the same convention.
The 7493 is the classic 4-bit binary ripple counter IC; 7492 is a divide-by-12 counter, and the other two option numbers aren't real ripple-counter parts.
Four 8K ROMs occupy 32K = 0x8000 bytes, i.e. addresses 0000H-7FFFH, so the first 4K-word RAM starts right after at 8000H and ends at 8000H+0FFFH = 8FFFH.

Computer organization covers how the architecture's specified features are actually implemented in hardware, visible to the system/hardware designer (developer), not the programmer/end user, which is the domain of computer architecture.

The dominant stored-program model underlying most general-purpose computers today is still the Von Neumann architecture, even though Harvard-style separate instruction/data paths appear inside CPU caches.
A row's bits are held in a latch (sense-amp/row buffer) so all bytes of that row can be read out together instead of being re-fetched one at a time.
Hit rate is defined as the fraction of memory accesses that are successfully satisfied (found) without a miss.

ASCII is the standard 8-bit (extended)/7-bit character encoding used to store text data; EBCDIC is also 8-bit but is IBM-specific and not the usual default answer, and the other two options are garbled non-standard names.
A stack pointer is the register that holds/points to the current top (here described as the 'beginning') of the stack in memory; it is not a subroutine-address storage location or a flag register.
The Intel 8080 is an 8-bit microprocessor with an 8-bit data bus to memory (its address bus is separately 16-bit).
A memory word's natural size is chosen to match the number of bits needed to represent an integer and an instruction, which is the classic definition of 'word' in computer organization texts.
A cache placed between the CPU and the MMU works on virtual addresses and is therefore called a logical (virtual) cache; a physical cache instead sits after the MMU and works on physical addresses.
RAID level 3 stripes data at the bit level across disks with a single dedicated parity disk, which is why it's called bit-interleaved parity (as in the standard OS textbook treatment).

The intended answer is J=1,K=1, the only input combination that makes a J-K flip-flop toggle, but OCR has merged options (c) and (d) into what's labelled 'B' here and dropped separate C/D keys entirely, so the printed lettering doesn't cleanly map to one choice; picking 'B' because 'J=1,K=1' literally appears inside its garbled text.

Pipelining is traditionally presented as a defining/enabling feature of RISC design (uniform, simple instructions pipeline cleanly), even though modern CISC chips pipeline too; that's the answer this style of question expects.
Miss rate is the fraction of memory accesses that fail to find the requested data (the complement of hit rate).
A floating-point number is normalized when there is no leading zero in the mantissa, i.e. its most significant bit is non-zero.
Putting four 4-bit registers onto a 4-line bus needs one 4-to-1 MUX per bit position (bit 0 of all four registers through one MUX, bit 1 through another, etc.), so 4 MUXes are required in total.
A memory-reference instruction's format is opcode plus an address field that specifies the memory operand's location.

Cycle stealing is the DMA mode where the controller takes the bus for just one word transfer at a time and then gives control back to the CPU, as opposed to burst transfer which holds the bus for a whole block.
Handshaking is the protocol where the receiving unit sends back an explicit acknowledgement control signal confirming it has received the data.
Linear search checks each of the n elements in the worst case, giving O(n) time.
Binary search halves the remaining search space each comparison, giving O(log2 n) time on a sorted array.
A singly linked list offers no random access, so finding an element requires traversing up to all n nodes, i.e. O(n).
With a doubly linked list you already have a pointer to the previous node, so deleting a node whose location is known is O(1); a singly linked list needs an O(n) scan to find the predecessor first.
Converting infix to postfix relies on a stack to hold operators until their precedence/associativity says they should be emitted.
Recursive calls save return addresses and local state on the call stack, so recursion is implemented using stacks.
Insertion at the rear and deletion from the front is exactly the FIFO behaviour that defines a queue.
A list that allows insertion and deletion at both ends (but not the middle) is a deque (double-ended queue).

Search in a binary search tree walks from root to leaf following one path, which is O(log2 n) when the tree is reasonably balanced; the true worst case for an unbalanced BST is O(n), but this style of question expects the typical/average-case answer.
Bubble sort's worst case (reverse-sorted input) does about n(n-1)/2 comparisons/swaps, i.e. O(n^2).
